(a) (p∧q)→p ≡ ¬(p∧q)∨p [7.1]
≡ (¬p∨¬q)∨p [DM]
≡ (¬p∨p)∨¬q [comm, assoc]
≡ T∨¬q [negation]
≡ T [domination].
(b) p→(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∨(p∨q) [7.1]
≡ (¬p∨p)∨q [assoc]
≡ T∨q [negation] ≡ T [domination].
(c) ¬p→(p→q) ≡ ¬¬p∨(¬p∨q) [7.1]
≡ (p∨¬p)∨q [DN, assoc]
≡ T∨q [negation] ≡ T [domination].
(d) (p∧q)→(p→q) ≡ ¬(p∧q)∨(¬p∨q) [7.1]
≡ (¬p∨¬q)∨(¬p∨q) [DM]
≡ (¬p∨¬p)∨(¬q∨q) [comm, assoc]
≡ ¬p∨T [idempotent, negation] ≡ T [domination].
(e) ¬(p→q)→p ≡ ¬¬(p→q)∨p [7.1]
≡ (¬p∨q)∨p [DN, 7.1]
≡ (¬p∨p)∨q [comm, assoc]
≡ T∨q [negation] ≡ T [domination].
(f) ¬(p→q)→¬q ≡ ¬¬(p→q)∨¬q [7.1]
≡ (¬p∨q)∨¬q [DN, 7.1]
≡ ¬p∨(q∨¬q) [assoc]

≡ ¬[(p∧¬p)∨(p∧q)]∨q [dist]
≡ ¬(p∧q)∨q [negation, identity]
≡ (¬p∨¬q)∨q [DM]
≡ ¬p∨(¬q∨q) [assoc]
≡ T [negation, domination].

≡ ¬[(p∨q)∧(¬p∨r)∧(¬q∨r)]∨r [7.1]

prompt:
Find the compound proposition Q constructed in Example 10 for the n-queens problem, and use it to find all the
    ways that n queens can be placed on an n × n chessboard,
    so that no queen can attack another when n is                ∗
    a) 2.               b) 3.              c) 4.
solution: Let p(i,j) mean a queen occupies row i, column j. Q is the conjunction of: for each row i, ∨ over j=1…n of p(i,j); for each pair of distinct squares sharing a row, column, or diagonal, the clause ¬p(i,j)∨¬p(k,l). These clauses enforce exactly one queen per row and no attacking pair. (a) n=2: either column choice in row 1 attacks both squares in row 2, so no solutions. (b) n=3: if row 1 uses the middle column no row-2 square remains; if it uses an end column, row 2 is forced to the opposite end and row 3 has no legal column. No solutions. (c) n=4: the column sequences by successive row are (2,4,1,3) and (3,1,4,2). Starting at columns 1 or 4 forces a dead end; starting at 2 or 3 forces the displayed sequence. Each has distinct columns and distinct row±column values, so no diagonal attack. ∎

prompt:
Show how the solution of a given 4 × 4 Sudoku puzzle
     can be found by solving a satisfiability problem.
solution: Let p(i,j,k) mean cell (i,j) contains k, for 1≤i,j,k≤4. Conjoin: (1) every cell has at least one k; (2) each cell has at most one k, using ¬p(i,j,k)∨¬p(i,j,l) for k≠l; (3) each row contains every k; (4) each column contains every k; (5) each of the four 2×2 blocks contains every k; (6) each given clue p(i,j,k). Row clauses are ∨ over j of p(i,j,k); column clauses are ∨ over i; block clauses are disjunctions over their four cells. A satisfying assignment is exactly a completed puzzle obeying all rules, because the clauses directly encode every rule. ∎

A statement is in prenex normal form (PNF) if and only if
it is of the form
           Q1 x1 Q2 x² ⋯ Qk xk P(x1 , x² , ... , xk ),
where each Qi , i = 1, 2, ... , k, is either the existential quantifier or the universal quantifier, and P(x1 , ... , xk ) is a predicate
involving no quantifiers. For example, ∃x∀y(P(x, y) ∧ Q(y)) is
in prenex normal form, whereas ∃xP(x) ∨ ∀xQ(x) is not (because the quantifiers do not all occur first).
     Every statement formed from propositional variables,
predicates, T, and F using logical connectives and quantifiers is equivalent to a statement in prenex normal form.
Exercise 51 asks for a proof of this fact.
solution: (a) If all x satisfy P and some y satisfies Q, that one y witnesses P(x)∧Q(y) for every x. Conversely, the right side makes P true for every x; choose any x in the nonempty domain and its y gives a witness to Q. (b) If P holds everywhere or Q has a witness, every x has an appropriate y. Conversely, if P fails at some x, its y must satisfy Q; if P never fails then ∀xP. Both equivalences follow. ∎

(b) If mathematics is not easy, not many students like logic. (c) Mathematics is not easy or logic is difficult. (d) Logic is not difficult or mathematics is not easy. (e) If not many students like logic, mathematics is not easy or logic is not difficult.
solution:
Let d=logic difficult,s=many students like logic,e=math easy. Premises d∨¬s and e→¬d.
(a) Valid: s→¬e.
| Step | Reason |
| ① d∨¬s | prem. |
| ② e→¬d | prem. |
| ③ s→d | comm, 7.1 of ① |
| ④ d→¬e | contrapositive and DN of ② |
| ⑤ s→¬e | Hypo. Syl. ③,④ |
∎
(b) ¬e→¬s is invalid; (c) ¬e∨d is invalid; (d) ¬d∨¬e is valid; (e) ¬s→(¬e∨¬d) is valid.
| Step | Reason |
| ① d=T,s=T,e=F | counterexample for (b) |
| ② d∨¬s=T and e→¬d=T; ¬e→¬s=F | premises true, conclusion false |
| ③ d=F,s=F,e=T | counterexample for (c) |
| ④ d∨¬s=T and e→¬d=T; ¬e∨d=F | premises true, conclusion false |
∎
For (d),(e):
| Step | Reason |
| ① e→¬d | prem. |
| ② ¬e∨¬d | 7.1 of ① |
| ③ ¬d∨¬e | comm of ②; proves (d) |
| ④ s∨(¬e∨¬d) | Addition of ②, comm |
| ⑤ ¬s→(¬e∨¬d) | 7.1, DN of ④; proves (e) |
∎

prompt:
Determine whether this argument, taken from Kalish and
     Montague [KaMo64], is valid.
           If Superman were able and willing to prevent evil,
           he would do so. If Superman were unable to prevent evil, he would be impotent; if he were unwilling

           does not exist.

| Step | Reason |
| ① (a∧w)→p | prem. |
| ② ¬a→i | prem. |
| ③ ¬w→m | prem. |
| ④ ¬p | prem. |
| ⑤ e→(¬i∧¬m) | prem. |
| ⑥ ¬(a∧w) | M.T. ①,④ |
| ⑦ ¬a∨¬w | DM of ⑥ |
| ⑧ a∨i | 7.1, DN of ② |
| ⑨ w∨m | 7.1, DN of ③ |
| ⑩ ¬w∨i | Resolution ⑦,⑧ |
| ⑪ i∨m | Resolution ⑩,⑨ |
| ⑫ ¬(¬i∧¬m) | DM, DN of ⑪ |
∎
| Step | Reason |
| ⑬ ¬e | M.T. ⑤,⑫ |
∎ Valid.
